title: Special Theory of Relativity
short_intro: The Special Theory of Relativity, formulated by Albert Einstein in 1905, redefines the concepts of space, time, mass, and energy based on the invariance of the speed of light. It operates on inertial reference frames moving at constant relative velocities.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Galilean transformations, Postulates of special relativity, Length contraction, Time dilation, Mass-energy equivalence at a basic level.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Lorentz transformations, Velocity addition theorem, Relativistic momentum and energy, Doppler effect in relativity, Proper time and spacetime interval.

prerequisites: Maxwell's equations and constancy of c

concept_notes.heading: Postulates of Special Relativity
bullets: The Principle of Relativity: All the laws of physics are the same in all inertial frames of reference.
The Constancy of the Speed of Light: The speed of light in vacuum is a universal constant (c) independent of the motion of the source or the observer.
These two postulates replace Galilean relativity and abandon the concept of the absolute luminiferous ether.

concept_notes.heading: Lorentz Transformations
bullets: Relates the space and time coordinates (x, y, z, t) of an event in frame S to (x', y', z', t') in frame S' moving with velocity v along the x-axis.
Equations: x' = gamma(x - vt), y' = y, z' = z, t' = gamma(t - vx/c²) where gamma = 1 / sqrt(1 - v²/c²).
Reduces to Galilean transformations in the limit v << c.

concept_notes.heading: Kinematic Consequences
bullets: Time Dilation: A clock moving relative to an observer runs slower than a clock at rest in the observer's frame by factor gamma. Proper time t_0 is the shortest measured interval.
Length Contraction: The length of an object moving at speed v is contracted along the direction of motion by factor 1/gamma. Proper length l_0 is the maximum length measured in the rest frame.
Relativity of Simultaneity: Events simultaneous in one inertial frame are generally not simultaneous in another moving inertial frame.

concept_notes.heading: Relativistic Dynamics and Energy
bullets: Relativistic Mass and Momentum: Momentum becomes p = gamma m_0 v, where m_0 is the rest mass.
Mass-Energy Equivalence: Total relativistic energy is given by E = gamma m_0 c² = sqrt(p²c² + m_0²c^4).
Rest Mass Energy: For a particle at rest (p=0), E_0 = m_0 c².

derivations.title: Time Dilation Derivation
derivations.conditions: Frame S' moves with constant velocity v along the x-axis relative to frame S.
steps: Consider a clock at rest in frame S' at position x'. The time interval between two ticks measured by a stationary observer in S' is the proper time interval: delta t_0 = t_2' - t_1'.
Using the inverse Lorentz transformation for time: t = gamma(t' + vx'/c²).
Calculate the time interval measured by an observer in frame S: delta t = t_2 - t_1 = gamma(t_2' - t_1') = gamma delta t_0.

derivations.title: Length Contraction Derivation
derivations.conditions: Rod of proper length l_0 is at rest in frame S'.
steps: The proper length measured in frame S' is l_0 = x_2' - x_1'.
To measure length in frame S, the coordinates of both ends x_1 and x_2 must be measured simultaneously (delta t = 0).
Using the Lorentz transformation x' = gamma(x - vt), apply it to both ends: l_0 = gamma(x_2 - x_1 - v(t_2 - t_1)). Since measurements are simultaneous in S (t_1 = t_2), l_0 = gamma(l).

graphs_and_experiments.title: Lorentz Factor (gamma) vs Velocity (v/c)
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A plot starting at (0, 1) remaining nearly flat up to v/c = 0.5 and then curving asymptotically upwards toward infinity as v/c approaches 1.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Shows that relativistic effects are negligible at low velocities (v << c) where gamma ~ 1, but diverge rapidly as velocity approaches the speed of light.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested conceptually in MCQ questions regarding the domain of applicability of classical mechanics versus relativity.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Muon Decay Experiment (Experimental Verification of Time Dilation)
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Atmospheric depth vs muon flux showing significantly higher muon detection at sea level than classical calculation predicts.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Unstable muons traveling at relativistic speeds have their lifetimes dilated, allowing them to reach the Earth's surface before decaying.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently asked descriptive and numerical question in PGT exams.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Minkowski Spacetime Diagram
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Ct vs x axes with worldlines of particles and the light cone defined by lines x = +/- ct.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Visualizes causal relationships, event intervals (spacelike, timelike, lightlike), and invariant spacetime intervals.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Used for conceptual questions on spacetime intervals and simultaneity.

solved_numericals.question: At what speed should a clock be moved so that it may appear to lose 1 minute in each day?
solution_steps: Proper time interval for one day: t_0 = 24 * 3600 s = 86400 s.
Dilated time interval: t = 86400 + 60 = 86460 s (since it loses time, t > t_0).
Using t = gamma t_0, we have t / t_0 = 1 / sqrt(1 - v²/c²) = 86460 / 86400.
Square both sides and solve for v/c: 1 - v²/c² = (86400 / 86460)² approx 1 - 2(60/86400) = 1 - 1/720.

solved_numericals.question: Find the momentum and kinetic energy of an electron (rest mass m_0 = 9.1 x 10^-31 kg) moving with a speed of 0.6c.
solution_steps: Calculate the Lorentz factor gamma: gamma = 1 / sqrt(1 - (0.6c)²/c²) = 1 / sqrt(1 - 0.36) = 1 / sqrt(0.64) = 1 / 0.8 = 1.25.
Calculate momentum p = gamma m_0 v = 1.25 * (9.1 x 10^-31 kg) * (0.6 * 3 x 10^8 m/s).
Calculate kinetic energy K = (gamma - 1)m_0 c² = (1.25 - 1) * (9.1 x 10^-31) * (3 x 10^8)².
solved_numericals.answer: Momentum = 2.05 x 10^-22 kg m/s, Kinetic Energy = 2.05 x 10^-14 J

solved_numericals.question: A particle has a total energy that is 3 times its rest mass energy. Find its speed and momentum.
solution_steps: Since E = gamma m_0 c², it follows that gamma = 3.
From gamma = 1 / sqrt(1 - v²/c²), we get 3 = 1 / sqrt(1 - v²/c²), so 1 - v²/c² = 1/9.
v²/c² = 8/9 => v = c * sqrt(8)/3 = 2sqrt(2)/3 c approx 0.943 c.
Momentum p = gamma m_0 v = 3 * m_0 * (2sqrt(2)/3 c) = 2sqrt(2) m_0 c.

assumptions_and_limitations: Assumption: Inertial frames move at constant relative velocities with no acceleration.
Limitation: Special relativity does not account for gravitational fields or accelerated frames; General Relativity is required for non-inertial systems and gravity.

common_misconceptions.wrong: An object's mass increases with speed according to relativistic mass m = gamma m_0.
common_misconceptions.correct: Modern physics prefers using invariant rest mass m_0, while momentum and energy increase with velocity.
common_misconceptions.why: Rest mass is an invariant scalar property; attributing speed dependence to mass causes confusion in dynamic equations.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Time actually stops for a photon traveling at the speed of light.
common_misconceptions.correct: The Lorentz transformation and time dilation equations are undefined (division by zero) for massless particles moving at c.
common_misconceptions.why: Photons do not possess a rest frame; proper time cannot be defined along a lightlike worldline.

quick_revision: Special relativity relies on the constancy of c and the equivalence of all inertial frames.
Time dilates (t = gamma t_0) and length contracts (l = l_0 / gamma) along the direction of relative motion.
Total energy and momentum are related by E² = p²c² + m_0²c^4.
